document_summary: PublicCEO news article (Feb. 24, 2026) on a Santa Ana, CA ordinance banning algorithmic rent-setting software, approved on first reading Feb. 17, 2026 with a final vote set for March 3, 2026.

rules.title: Santa Ana ban on algorithmic rent-setting software
rules.requirement: Prohibits the sale, licensing, provision and use of certain algorithmic rent-setting software for residential rental properties, i.e. devices that set rents using nonpublic competitor data. Tenants may sue for injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties, and need only prove the landlord used the prohibited technology, not intentional collusion.
rules.key_value: Ban on sale, licensing, provision and use of algorithmic rent-setting software using nonpublic competitor data
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental property within Santa Ana city limits.
rules.exemptions: Pricing software that relies solely on publicly available data, aggregate historical data, or tools used to comply with affordable housing program requirements.
rules.interaction: Structured to operate alongside existing and proposed state antitrust laws while providing stronger local protections.
rules.citation: Santa Ana Municipal Code, algorithmic rent-setting software ordinance (ordinance number and section not stated in source)
rules.quoted_span: The ordinance, approved on Tuesday, Feb. 17, for a first reading and set for a final vote on March 3, prohibits the sale, licensing, provision and use of certain algorithmic rent-setting software for residential rental properties.
rules.conflict_note: Open question: this capture reports only first-reading approval (Feb. 17, 2026) and a scheduled final vote (March 3, 2026); it does not confirm final adoption or give an effective date.
rules.extraction_notes: Status marked pending because the document shows only a first reading and a scheduled final vote; the outcome is not in this capture, and the ordinance may have since been adopted. No effective date or adoption date is stated, so both are null. Civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, plus attorney's fees, are noted but not used as the key value.
